abstract: The detection of mechanical stress is essential for a wide range of physiological functions in humans, including touch sensation, hearing, and the maintenance of vascular myogenic tone. PIEZO1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that is widely expressed in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells and plays critical physiological roles in multiple organs. However, the electrophysiological properties of endogenous PIEZO1-mediated mechanosensitive currents have not been systematically compared across different human cell types under identical experimental conditions. Here, the author compared the electrophysiological properties of endogenous human PIEZO1 (hPIEZO1) currents in four cultured human cell types: human aortic endothelial cells, human brain capillary endothelial cells, human fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and human osteoblast-like MG63 cells. Under whole-cell patch-clamp conditions, application of the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 robustly activated hPIEZO1-like currents in all four cell types. In excised outside-out patch recordings, application of positive pressure to membrane patches from these cells also elicited PIEZO1-like channel currents, which were markedly potentiated by Yoda1 and effectively inhibited by gadolinium, a non-selective cation channel blocker. Furthermore, the unitary current amplitudes of single channel events evoked by mechanical stimulation were comparable to those elicited by Yoda1 across all four cell types. Collectively, these findings provide electrophysiological evidence that endogenous PIEZO1 functions as a mechanosensor in diverse human cell types and suggest that PIEZO1 contributes to mechanically regulated physiological processes in multiple human organs.
